<ExternalIntegrationHeader integration={{"name":"Tasmota","description":"Control your Tasmota devices locally over MQTT or HTTP: relays, lights, energy, sensors.","owner":"gboulvin","owner_avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/78817935?v=4","repo_url":"https://github.com/gboulvin/Gladys-Tasmota","cover_url":"https://integration-store-storage.gladysassistant.com/covers/gboulvin--Gladys-Tasmota.png","type":"device","version":"1.1.0","gladys_version":">=5.3.0","stars":0,"pushed_at":"2026-10-26T08:43:51Z"}} />

Control your [Tasmota](https://tasmota.github.io/) devices from Gladys, **100 % locally**: plugs,
relays, bulbs and LED strips, dimmers, shutters, fans, energy meters and sensors. No cloud.

## What you get

- **Automatic discovery** over MQTT (`LWT`, `Status 0` and the Tasmota native discovery) and over
  HTTP (a list of addresses, or a scan of an IP range).
- Every device is identified by its **MAC address**: renaming it, changing its topic or its IP,
  or moving it from HTTP to MQTT keeps the same Gladys device and its history.
- **Relays** (`POWER1`…`POWER8`), **lights** (on/off, brightness, RGB color, white temperature,
  effects and their speed), **fans** (`FanSpeed`), **shutters** (open / close / stop, position).
- **Energy metering**: power, apparent and reactive power, voltage, current, energy today,
  yesterday and total (the total is a cumulative index, usable by the Gladys energy monitoring),
  multi-channel meters included.
- **Sensors**: temperature, humidity, pressure, illuminance, CO2, VOC, PM2.5 / PM10, distance,
  UV index, soil moisture, analog inputs, pulse counters, switch inputs, chip temperature, Wi-Fi
  signal and uptime.
- **Scene triggers**: button pressed (single, double, triple… hold), switch input changed,
  RF code received (Sonoff RF Bridge), IR code received, device online / offline.
- **Scene actions**: send any Tasmota command (Backlog, RfSend, IRSend, Rule…), turn a relay on
  for a while, make a light blink, restart a device.
- **Dashboard widgets**: fleet overview, device card, energy card.
- A **"Local" badge** on each device, orange when the broker is down and commands fall back to
  HTTP, red when the device is unreachable.

## Choose how the devices talk to Gladys

The Configuration screen starts with **Step 1 — Connection mode**, followed by three blocks.
Gladys shows every block at once: **fill in only the block of the option you chose**, the
others are ignored and can stay empty. The status at the top of the screen always says which
option is active and what is missing.

| Connection mode                                | Fill in | You need                        |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ------- | ------------------------------- |
| Option 1 — My existing MQTT broker             | block 1 | the address and credentials     |
| Option 2 — Dedicated broker deployed by Gladys | block 2 | nothing (optional password)     |
| Option 3 — No MQTT, HTTP only                  | block 3 | the IP addresses of the devices |

### Option 1 — My existing MQTT broker

For instance the broker of the Gladys **MQTT** integration, which already runs on the Gladys
host (port 1883, with the user and password shown on the page of that integration).

1. **Connection mode**: _Option 1 — My existing MQTT broker_.
2. **Block 1 — Broker URL**: `mqtt://<IP of the broker>:1883` — use the LAN IP address, not
   `localhost` (the integration runs in its own container).
3. **Block 1 — Broker user** and **Broker password**, then save.
4. On each Tasmota device: **Configuration → MQTT**, enter the same host, port, user and
   password.

### Option 2 — Dedicated broker deployed by the integration

1. **Connection mode**: _Option 2 — Dedicated broker deployed by the integration_.
2. **Block 2 — Password of the devices**: optional, leave it empty to have one generated.
   Save: the integration starts its own Mosquitto container; block 2 shows the address and
   port the devices must use (user `tasmota`).
3. Run the **Option 2 — Get the command for the devices** action (type the IP address of
   Gladys): it gives a ready-to-paste line, e.g.
   `Backlog MqttHost 192.168.1.10; MqttPort 41883; MqttUser tasmota; MqttPassword …`.
4. Paste it in the **Console** of each Tasmota device. The device restarts and appears in Gladys.

### MQTT topics (options 1 and 2)

Keep **%prefix%/%topic%/**, the Tasmota default, unless you changed the Full Topic of your
devices to `%topic%/%prefix%/`.

### Option 3 — No MQTT, HTTP only

1. **Connection mode**: _Option 3 — No MQTT, HTTP only_.
2. **Block 3 — HTTP addresses**: `192.168.1.20, 192.168.1.30-45` (or use the **Scan an IP
   range** action).
3. **Web user** (`admin`) and **Web password**: only if a web admin password is set on the
   devices. The devices are read every **HTTP refresh interval** seconds (30 by default).

Block 3 also works with options 1 and 2, for the few devices that do not use MQTT. A device
found over HTTP that later connects to the broker switches to MQTT by itself; the **Move a
device to MQTT** action sends it the broker settings for you.

## Add the devices

Open the **Discovery** tab of the integration: the devices found appear there, with their
features. Click **Add**, choose the room, done. When a device gains a feature (a sensor plugged
in, a new firmware), an **Update** button appears.

## Migrate from the native Tasmota integration

Coming from the Tasmota integration built into Gladys? Gladys can move each device to this
integration **in one click**, keeping its state history, the scenes and dashboards that use it,
its room and the thermostat settings that point to it. The old device is then deleted.

This requires a Gladys version that shows a **Migrate** button on the devices of the native
Tasmota integration ([GladysAssistant/Gladys#3256](https://github.com/GladysAssistant/Gladys/pull/3256)).
Until then, both integrations can run side by side.

1. **Connect this integration to the same broker** as the native one: option 1, with in block 1
   the address and credentials of the Gladys MQTT integration's broker. Both integrations can
   listen to the same devices at the same time, and nothing changes on the devices. HTTP devices:
   list their addresses in block 3.
2. In the **Discovery** tab, **add the device**, and keep the native one for now.
3. **Migrate right away.** When both devices record states in parallel, Gladys keeps the old
   history only up to the first state of the new device: the states recorded twice in between
   are dropped. The longer you wait, the longer that period.
4. Open the native **Tasmota** integration, **Devices** tab, and click **Migrate** on the device.
   Pick its new version: the list groups the devices by integration and shows their room.
5. **Check the pairing of the features**, then confirm. Most of them are paired automatically
   (relays, lights, power, voltage, current, energy of the day, temperature, humidity…). Two cases
   are paired by hand:
   - **Energy total**: pair it with _Energy total_. Gladys warns that the types differ (`energy`
     in the native integration, `index` here, the type the energy monitoring relies on); the
     values in kWh are the same, you can confirm.
   - **A light shown as a switch**: the native integration only recognises a few light modules,
     the others came in as a switch. This integration recognises the light: pair _Switch_ with
     _Light_.

   A feature left unpaired loses its history, and the scenes that use it must be edited.

6. On a large history the migration takes a few minutes: follow it in **Settings → Tasks**. If it stops, run it again: it only moves what is left.

Once every device is migrated, the native Tasmota integration has no device left.

## Actions of the Configuration screen

- **Test the connection** — broker state and number of devices online.
- **Option 2 — Get the command for the devices** — the console line for the dedicated broker.
- **Add an HTTP device** / **Scan an IP range** — find devices over HTTP (1024 addresses max).
- **Identify a light** — the light blinks twice and goes back to its state. Relays never blink
  (they may drive a heater).
- **Send a command** — any Tasmota command, the answer is shown under the button.
- **Restart a device**.
- **Move a device to MQTT** — sends `MqttHost`, `MqttPort`, `MqttUser`, `MqttPassword`.

## Scenes

Under the **Integrations** category of the scene editor (Gladys 5.1 or later):

| Trigger                         | Tasmota setting needed                                | Variables          |
| ------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | ------------------ |
| Tasmota button pressed          | `SetOption73 1` (buttons decoupled from the relays)   | `button`, `action` |
| Tasmota switch input changed    | `SetOption114 1` (switches decoupled from the relays) | `switch`, `action` |
| RF code received                | an RF Bridge (`RfReceived`)                           | `code`, `rf_key`   |
| IR code received                | an IR receiver (`IrReceived`)                         | `code`, `protocol` |
| Tasmota device online / offline | none (LWT over MQTT, failed polls over HTTP)          | `status`           |

Every filter is optional: left empty, it matches everything. Read the values in the next actions
with `{{triggerEvent.data.code}}`, for instance.

Actions: **Send a Tasmota command** (outputs `answered` and `response`), **Turn a relay on for a
while** (the device turns it off by itself, up to 360 s), **Make a Tasmota light blink**,
**Restart a Tasmota device**.

The states themselves (a relay, a temperature…) are regular device features: use the standard
"Device state" trigger and "Control a device" action of Gladys for them.

## Dashboard

- **Tasmota devices** — devices count, online and offline, broker connection, state of each
  device, a **Refresh** button.
- **Tasmota device** — pick a device: its main live values, IP, firmware, Wi-Fi signal, uptime,
  and **Toggle**, **Identify** (lights) and **Restart** buttons.
- **Tasmota energy** — pick a metering device: 24-hour power chart, live power, voltage, current,
  energy today, yesterday and total.

## Troubleshooting

- **Nothing in Discovery (MQTT)**: check the broker URL uses the LAN IP, and that the devices
  show "MQTT connected" in their console. Click **Scan** in the Discovery tab: every known device
  is asked its status again.
- **A device asks for a password (HTTP)**: fill the Web user and password in the configuration,
  or in the fields of the Add / Scan actions.
- **Buttons do not trigger scenes**: send `SetOption73 1` to the device (and `SetOption114 1` for
  switch inputs).
- **Logs**: open the integration logs from Gladys; set `LOG_LEVEL=debug` for the full detail.

## Configuration settings

These are the settings Tasmota asks for in its configuration screen in Gladys.

| Setting | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Step 1 — Choose how your devices connect | `section` | No | Option 1: you already have an MQTT broker (for instance the one of the Gladys MQTT integration): fill in block 1 with its address and credentials. Option 2: you have no broker: the integration deploys a dedicated Mosquitto container, fill in block 2 only. Option 3: no MQTT, the devices are read over HTTP: fill in block 3 only. The blocks of the other options are ignored, you can leave them empty. |
| Connection mode | `select` | Yes |  |
| Block 1 — My existing MQTT broker (option 1 only) | `section` | No | The address and credentials of your broker. With the broker of the Gladys MQTT integration: mqtt:\/\/\<IP of Gladys>:1883 and the user and password shown on the page of that integration. Use the LAN IP address, not localhost: the integration runs in its own container. Your Tasmota devices must point to the same broker (Configuration > MQTT on each device). |
| Broker URL | `string` | No |  |
| Broker user | `string` | No |  |
| Broker password | `secret` | No |  |
| Block 2 — Dedicated broker deployed by the integration (option 2 only) | `section` | No | Nothing to install: when you save, the integration starts its own Mosquitto container. Your devices connect to \{\{gladys_host\}\}, port \{\{port:mqtt\}\}, user tasmota, with the password below (leave it empty to have one generated). Then run the "Get the command for the devices" action: it gives the line to paste in the console of each Tasmota device. |
| Password of the devices | `secret` | No | Optional: leave empty to have one generated. |
| MQTT topics (options 1 and 2) | `section` | No | Keep the default unless you changed the Full Topic of your devices. |
| Tasmota FullTopic | `select` | Yes |  |
| Block 3 — HTTP devices (option 3, optional with options 1 and 2) | `section` | No | Devices read over HTTP, every few seconds. Required with option 3; with options 1 and 2, only for devices that do not use MQTT. List their addresses (or use the "Scan an IP range" action). Web user and password: only if a web admin password is set on the devices. |
| HTTP addresses | `string` | No | IPs, host names or ranges, separated by commas. |
| Web user | `string` | No |  |
| Web password | `secret` | No |  |
| HTTP refresh interval (s) | `number` | No | How often HTTP devices are read (MQTT devices push their changes). |

## How to install Tasmota in Gladys

1. In Gladys, open **Integrations**: Tasmota appears in the catalog, next to the native integrations, with a community badge.
2. Click **Install**. Gladys pulls the Docker image (`ghcr.io/gboulvin/gladys-tasmota:1.1.0`), starts it in a sandbox isolated from the core, and generates the integration's interface (devices, discovery and configuration).
3. Open the **Configuration** screen of the integration, fill in the settings, and save.
4. You can also install it directly from its repository URL: [https://github.com/gboulvin/Gladys-Tasmota](https://github.com/gboulvin/Gladys-Tasmota).

Tasmota requires Gladys `>=5.3.0`. The catalog inside Gladys refreshes every hour, so a new version becomes available at most one hour after its release.

Not running Gladys yet? It is free and open source: [follow the installation guide](/docs/) to get started.

## About external integrations

Tasmota is an **external integration**: a community integration packaged as a Docker container and published on GitHub, that Gladys installs in one click and runs in a sandbox isolated from its core. It is published and maintained by [gboulvin](https://github.com/gboulvin), not by the Gladys core team.
